newsitem.title: USA: GM shuts down second assembly plant due to strike.
newsitem.headline: GM shuts down second assembly plant due to strike.

text.p: General Motors Corp. said a transmission plant strike forced it to close a second assembly plant Thursday as the walkout in Warren, Mich., threatened to disrupt nearly all of GM's North American production.

GM spokesman Thomas Klipstine said the automaker sent more than 3,000 workers home from its Orion, Mich., car assembly plant Thursday afternoon. GM idled 2,700 at its Buick City car plant in Flint, Mich., at the end of Wednesday's shifts.

Other GM plants also in immediate danger of running out of transmissions and other parts made at the strike-bound Warren Powertrain Division plant include car plants in Lansing, Mich., and Oshawa, Ontario.
The Warren plant in suburban Detroit produces automatic transmissions for front-wheel-drive cars and a number of other parts, including wheels and suspension control arms.
The Flint and Orion plants, also in southeastern Mich., are supplied on a "just-in-time" basis that keeps their stocks of transmissions low.
The Flint plant builds Buick LaSabre and Pontiac Bonneville sedans. The Orion plant also builds the Bonneville, as well as Buick Riviera, Oldsmobile Aurora and Eighty Eight cars.
Bargainers for United Auto Workers Local 909 and General Motors Corp. resumed negotiations Thursday morning in an effort to end the strike.
GM spokeswoman Darla Park said the two sides had talked until about midnight last night.

About 2,700 UAW members walked off the job at midnight Tuesday when talks failed to produce a new contract at the Warren plant, which produces automatic transmissions for GM cars and light trucks, including minivans.

The union wants GM to add more employees to reduce overtime burdens and limit outsourcing of work. GM is trying to avoid hiring more employees as it seeks to reduce its overall labour force and improve manufacturing efficiencies.
Jim Marcum, financial secretary for UAW Local 909, said strikers are not happy about forcing other union members off the job but were standing firm against GM.
"It's an unfortunate byproduct," he said. "We don't want other people to be out of work because of us. That's never the union's intention."
